intro: Looking for addiction counselling near you usually means something has reached a point where you want help close to home, whether the addiction is to alcohol, drugs, gambling or something else. You may be searching for yourself, or for someone you care about, and wondering who locally can help you understand the pattern and start to change it. We introduce people to UK counsellors who work with addiction, and the counsellor quotes you directly, so you can decide what suits you.
need_heading: What people searching for addiction counselling usually need
need_lead: Most people typing "addiction counselling near me" want someone local they can talk to about a habit that has become hard to control, without judgement.
needs: You have realised that your drinking, drug use or gambling has moved beyond something you can manage alone and you want to talk it through with someone nearby.
You are worried about a partner, family member or friend and want local counselling that can help them, and you, understand what is going on.
You have tried to stop before and want help understanding the patterns that keep pulling you back, rather than another attempt on willpower alone.
You are unsure whether you need counselling, medical help or both, and want to speak to a counsellor who understands addiction and can point you in the right direction.
You want support that fits around work, caring responsibilities or family life, which is why finding someone near you matters.
context: "Counsellor" and "psychotherapist" are not protected titles in the UK, so anyone can use them. To protect yourself, look for a practitioner on a register accredited by the Professional Standards Authority, such as BACP, UKCP or NCPS. Practitioner psychologists, who use titles such as clinical or counselling psychologist, must be registered with the HCPC.

Accredited registers require training, supervision, a code of ethics and a complaints procedure. A good therapist will explain their approach, confidentiality and its limits in the first session, so you know where you stand before you commit.
tell_heading: What to tell us when you enquire
tell: Say which addiction is involved, such as alcohol, drugs, gambling or something else, so we can introduce you to a counsellor who works with it.
Mention whether the enquiry is for you or for someone else, and whether that person knows you are looking.
Describe how long the issue has been going on and what you have already tried, in your own words.
Say whether you think medical help might be needed, for example whether a detox could be relevant for alcohol.
Explain any preferences about the counsellor, such as whether you would like to see someone in person locally or talk by phone or online.
Include anything that would make it easier to attend, such as work hours, caring responsibilities or difficulty travelling far.
questions: What is your training and experience in working with addiction?
Are you on a register accredited by the Professional Standards Authority, and which one?
How would you describe your approach to addiction counselling?
What are the limits of confidentiality, and when would you share information with others?
Would you work alongside other support, such as AA or medical help, and how?
How do you involve family or partners in the work, if at all?

faqs.q: Do I need to be sure I have an addiction before I enquire?
faqs.a: No. Many people get in touch when they are worried about their drinking, drug use or gambling but are not sure how serious it is. A counsellor can talk it through with you and help you work out what kind of support makes sense.

faqs.q: Can counselling help if I also need medical support?
faqs.a: Counselling can sit alongside medical help. For alcohol in particular, a medical detox may be needed, and a counsellor should be able to discuss this with you and encourage you to seek appropriate medical advice. Groups such as AA can also complement therapy.

faqs.q: What if the person who needs help is a family member, not me?
faqs.a: You can still enquire on their behalf and ask about family support, which often helps. The counsellor can explain what is possible and whether the person themselves would need to be involved.

faqs.q: How do I know a counsellor is properly trained?
faqs.a: Because "counsellor" is not a protected title, check whether the practitioner is on a register accredited by the Professional Standards Authority, such as BACP, UKCP or NCPS. Accredited registers require training, supervision, a code of ethics and a complaints procedure, so it is worth asking before you begin.
